newsitem.title: ROMANIA: CEAUSESCU HEIR FUNERAL DRAWS BIG BUCHAREST CROWDS.
newsitem.headline: CEAUSESCU HEIR FUNERAL DRAWS BIG BUCHAREST CROWDS.

text.p: Thousands of Romanians attended the funeral of Nicu Ceausescu, youngest son of late communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, who was buried near the graves of his parents in a Bucharest cemetery on Sunday.

Relatives and friends gathered to pay their last respects to Nicu, seen as his father's political heir before Ceausescu and his wife Elena were ousted and shot in a December 1989 revolt which ended their ruthless 24-year rule.
Nicu, 45, a hard-drinking playboy, died in a Vienna hospital on Thursday from acute liver disease and friends flew his body back home one day later for burial.
Several thousand curious crowds thronged the northwest Ghencea cemetery on Sunday for a glimpse of Nicu's coffin, wrapped in Romania's red-yellow-and-blue national flag.
Members of the once powerful Ceausescu clan surrounded Nicu's elder brother Valentin and his sister Zoe as Orthodox priests held the two-hour funeral service.
Nicu was buried 100 yards (metres) away from the tombs of his parents, who were shot by firing squad on Christmas 1989.
Many Romanians harbour ambivalent feelings about the Ceausescu era and their fall.
"God rest his soul. His biggest sin was that he was his father's son," said one weeping woman, while dozens of security guards tried to keep the crowd under control.

Adrian Paunescu, a former Ceausescu court poet, recited an ode to "Prince" Nicu. Paunescu runs for president for the Socialist Labour Party, heir to the former Communist Party, in November 3 polls, which coincide with parliamentary elections.
"Where has Romanian industry gone, where's our daily bread...where's justice the people?" ran a dirge sung near Nicu's grave by a group of musicians led by Paunescu.
Living standards are lower and many say the true story of the 1989 revolt, seen by many as a coup by former communists who have held power ever since, has yet to be told.

Political analysts say former communists around Paunescu are trying to capitalise ahead of November's polls on popular discontent with growing poverty and corruption which have marked Romania's painful transition towards a free market.
Since the revolution, the Ceausescu family have kept a low profile and stayed away from politics.
Nicu was arrested during the revolution and convicted to 20 years in jail for ordering the repression of protests in the Transylvanian city of Sibiu where he was communist party boss.
Nicu always protested his innocence, saying he had left town before troops shot dead 91 people and wounded about 200.
He was paroled in 1992, after courts quashed his initial conviction. He served out a lesser sentence for illegal gun possession.
People in Sibiu remember Nicu for trying to oppose his father's belt-tightening policies. Some in his own generation see him as a liberal who snubbed hardliners around his father.
